- If sentiment is consistently negative or low (≤0.33) over recent days, reduce forecast slope or shift mean downward to avoid over-optimism.  
- If model shows strong upward trend (e.g., >90.00) with recent sentiment neutral or positive, check for overshoot — cap or adjust upward momentum if true price drops sharply.  
- If true price exhibits sharp downward spikes after recent highs, model may be lagging — adjust forecast to reflect recent volatility or add early correction factor.  
- When sentiment is mixed or volatile (alternating 0.33–1.00), avoid smooth linear extrapolation — introduce stochastic or stepwise adjustments to reflect sentiment shifts.  
- If model consistently overpredicts by 2–5% relative to true price, apply a downward bias correction, especially after sentiment dips below 0.67.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true price deviates >10% from forecast in first 5–7 days, consider mean reversion or volatility-adjusted baseline — don’t assume trend continues.  
- If sentiment is high (≥0.80) and model is flat or rising slowly, consider upward bias — but cap at 10–15% above recent high to avoid overcorrection.  
- If true price drops sharply after a spike, model may be “stuck” in prior peak — apply lag correction: reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days if sentiment turns negative.
